summary: This informational document defines vendor-specific RADIUS attributes from Cisco's space for delivering keying material securely and strongly authenticating any RADIUS message. They have been implemented by multiple vendors. It documents existing practice and is not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS is a way for network gear to check who may log in. These Cisco-defined extra fields let it hand over secret keys safely and prove messages are genuine.

questions: how does radius deliver keys securely
subtitle: Secure attributes for delivering cryptographic keys and authenticating RADIUS messages.

tldr.problem: RADIUS servers need a secure, standardized way to deliver cryptographic keying material (such as keys generated during EAP authentication) to network access points, and to prove that RADIUS messages are genuine and have not been modified.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6218 defines three Cisco vendor-specific RADIUS attributes: Keying-Material (which encrypts keys using AES Key Wrap), MAC-Randomizer (which adds randomness to prevent reply attacks), and Message-Authentication-Code (which signs messages with HMAC).
tldr.outcome: These attributes have been implemented by multiple vendors and provide stronger protection than earlier approaches like MS-MPPE-Keys, while remaining compatible with standard RADIUS.

today: RFC 6218 is Informational and describes existing vendor-specific practice implemented by multiple vendors. It has not been obsoleted. These attributes represent a stronger alternative to earlier RADIUS key distribution methods.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6218 defines vendor-specific RADIUS attributes from Cisco's space (Vendor ID 9) for two purposes: securely delivering cryptographic keying material and authenticating RADIUS messages to prevent spoofing. RADIUS is the protocol used in remote access and wireless networks to check user credentials and configure network access.

In many deployments, a RADIUS server performs EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) authentication with a user or device, and as a byproduct, generates cryptographic keying material (such as a Master Session Key) that the server must deliver to a network access point (like a wireless access point or VPN concentrator). The access point uses this key to protect traffic with the user's device. RFC 2548 and RFC 3579 defined earlier attributes for this purpose, but they had limitations. RFC 6218 provides attributes with stronger protection and more flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone logs in over a wireless network, the login server generates a secret key that both the user's device and the wireless access point need to know. These attributes let the server send that key safely to the access point.

sections.title: Attributes Overview
sections.content:
RFC 6218 defines three vendor-specific sub-attributes, all transmitted within RADIUS Vendor-Specific Attributes (Type 26 with Vendor ID 9). Each attribute has a String-ID field that begins with 'radius:' and a sub-type of 1.

The Keying-Material attribute transfers cryptographic keys from a RADIUS server to a client. It encrypts the key data using AES Key Wrap, a standard key encryption algorithm. The MAC-Randomizer attribute provides a 32-octet random number to prevent replay attacks. The Message-Authentication-Code attribute signs the entire RADIUS message using a keyed hash function (HMAC or CMAC), so the receiver can verify the message has not been modified and came from the expected peer.
sections.plainLanguage: These three attributes work together: one sends secret keys encrypted, one adds random noise to prevent replaying old messages, and one proves the message wasn't changed.

sections.title: Keying-Material Attribute
sections.content:
The Keying-Material attribute carries an encrypted key and metadata about it. The String-ID is 'radius:app-key='. Inside the attribute, fields specify an App ID (the type of key: 0 = reserved, 1 = EAP Master Session Key), a KEK ID (identifying which key-encrypting-key was used), a KM ID (identifying the keying material itself), a Lifetime (validity period in seconds), an IV (initialization vector), and the encrypted key data.

The Enc Type field specifies the encryption algorithm: currently, only Enc Type 0 (AES Key Wrap with 128-bit KEK per RFC 3394) is defined and mandatory. AES Key Wrap is a standard algorithm that takes a 128-bit or larger encryption key and wraps (encrypts) an arbitrary key with it, producing a result slightly longer than the input. For the EAP Master Session Key application, the KM ID is set to 0.

Crucially, any RADIUS message containing a Keying-Material attribute MUST also include a Message-Authentication-Code attribute, and must not include any other attribute (such as MS-MPPE-Send-Key from RFC 2548) that encapsulates the same keying material.
sections.plainLanguage: The Keying-Material attribute is a locked box: it says what kind of key is inside, how long the key is good for, and which lock was used to seal it. Only someone who knows the matching key can open it.

sections.title: MAC-Randomizer and Message-Authentication-Code
sections.content:
The MAC-Randomizer attribute contains a 32-octet random number that satisfies randomness requirements from RFC 4086. It must be present in any message that includes a Message-Authentication-Code attribute. The random value is filled in before the MAC is computed and should be placed at the beginning of the RADIUS message if possible.

The Message-Authentication-Code attribute signs the message to prove authenticity and prevent tampering. It has a MAC Type field specifying the algorithm (minimum requirement is HMAC-SHA-1, but HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-512, CMAC-AES-128, CMAC-AES-192, and CMAC-AES-256 are also defined), a 16-octet MAC Key ID (similar to KEK ID), and the MAC value itself. The MAC is computed over the entire RADIUS packet except the Request or Response Authenticator header field, using a shared secret as the key.

For requests, the MAC is computed as MAC = HASH-ALG(Key, Type + Identifier + Length + Attributes). For responses, the responder should include the MAC-Randomizer from the request if present. Both the MAC field and any Message-Authenticator field must be zero-filled when the hash is calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: The random number prevents an attacker from taking an old message and replaying it. The message authentication code proves someone with the right secret key created the message.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 6218 recommends that RADIUS implementations use two separate cryptographic keys: one for key encryption (KEK) and one for message authentication (MAC key). These keys MUST be different from each other and independent of the standard RADIUS shared secret, so compromising one does not break everything. The keys should be provisioned out-of-band and must not be derived from a password.

To prevent collision attacks, the same MAC key should not be used with more than 2^(n/2) messages, where n is the length of the MAC in octets (for example, with HMAC-SHA-1's 20-octet output, that is 2^80 messages). If a message contains the Keying-Material attribute alongside a weaker key-transport attribute carrying the same key, breaking the weaker attribute could enable a known-plaintext attack on the KEK.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementers must be careful to use strong, independent keys for each purpose, and not to mix this new method with old, weaker approaches in the same message.
